title: Fluids: Pressure, Buoyancy and Flow

cards.h: Why does a ship float and a dam get thicker?
cards.b:
A steel ship weighs thousands of tonnes yet floats. A dam is far thicker at the bottom than the top. A small push on a car jack lifts a whole car. Aeroplanes stay up on air that you cannot see.

All of these are the physics of fluids: liquids and gases, things that flow. Their key ideas are pressure, buoyancy and flow speed.

Pressure

P = F / A

The unit is the pascal (Pa): one newton per square metre. A sharp knife cuts because a modest force is squeezed onto a tiny area. A camel's wide feet stop it sinking in sand for the opposite reason.

Air presses on us too. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101,000 Pa, called one atmosphere. We do not feel it because the fluids inside us push outward equally.

Pressure in a liquid

P = (density) x g x h

Deeper means more fluid above pressing down. For water, density is 1000 kg per cubic metre, so every 10 m of depth adds about one atmosphere. That is why divers feel pressure on their ears, and why dam walls are built thicker at the base.

Notice that only depth matters, not the width of the container.

cards.h: Pascal's law and the hydraulic lift
cards.b:
Blaise Pascal (1650s) found that pressure applied to a confined fluid is passed on equally in every direction. A small piston pushing on a small area creates a pressure; the same pressure on a big piston gives a big force.

With areas 0.01 and 0.1 square metres, a 100 N push becomes 1000 N. This is how car jacks, garage lifts and the brakes of vehicles work. (You gain force, not energy: the small piston moves ten times farther.)

Archimedes of Syracuse (around 250 BCE) found that a body in a fluid feels an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside.

Buoyant force

F = (fluid density) x V x g

If this force beats the body's weight, it floats. A steel ship floats because its hollow shape displaces a huge volume of water, so its average density is less than water's. The same steel as a solid block would sink.

For a steady flow of liquid in a pipe, what goes in must come out: A x v is constant. Narrow the pipe and the water speeds up, as when you put a thumb over a hose.

Daniel Bernoulli (1738) showed that where a fluid moves faster, its pressure is lower:

Bernoulli

P + (1/2) density v squared + density g h = constant

This helps explain lift on an aircraft wing, spray bottles and the way a curveball curves.

P = density x g x h = 1000 x 9.8 x 10 = 98,000 Pa, about one atmosphere added by the water.

Total pressure at 10 m = surface air pressure + this = 101,000 + 98,000, nearly 2 atmospheres.

Buoyancy check: a 0.002 cubic metre (2 litre) bottle, fully under water, feels an upthrust of 1000 x 0.002 x 9.8 = 19.6 N, which is why it pops upward when you let go.

• 'Heavy things sink, light things float.' It is about density. A huge ship floats; a small steel pin sinks.
  • 'Water pressure depends on how much water there is.' It depends on depth. A deep narrow tube and a wide lake of the same depth give the same pressure.
  • 'Faster air pushes harder.' The reverse: faster fluid has lower pressure along a streamline.

The Bhakra Dam is thicker at its base since the water pressure there is much greater. India's hydropower and irrigation dams, from Hirakud to Sardar Sarovar, are designed with the P = density x g x h equation in mind.

The Indian Navy's ships, including the aircraft carrier INS Vikrant (commissioned 2022), float by Archimedes' principle: the carrier displaces water equal to its own huge weight.

• Pressure P = F/A; in a liquid P = density x g x h.
  • Pascal's law: pressure in a closed fluid spreads equally, giving hydraulic force multiplication.
  • Buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced.
  • Faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli).

Think about it

1. Why does a hot-air balloon rise, in terms of buoyancy?
2. Why is it harder to open a door to a pressurised cabin than an ordinary door?
